assessment.nobel_worthiness: The random-coefficients discrete-choice demand framework (BLP) and the dynamic oligopoly estimation methods that followed turned structural industrial organisation into a routine empirical tool. They are used for merger review, antitrust, trade and environmental policy. The work has high methodological and applied impact well beyond IO.
assessment.attribution: The core BLP contribution is cleanly attributable to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also has a separate line of work on dynamic games and estimation. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made real but more distinct contributions, so the three-person limit forces a choice.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers date from the 1990s. Several decades of use, extension and validation make this fully mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to credit Bresnahan or Reiss for the earlier empirical-IO foundations.
The scope of the prize (demand estimation versus dynamic games) is a judgment call.
Competing econometrics and IO candidates may be seen as having similar methodological claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade models changed how trade theory is understood. They explain selection, exporter premia and gains from trade through reallocation, and they connect closely to quantitative and empirical work. Helpman's earlier contributions to monopolistic-competition trade theory add to the case.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central theoretical contribution, and Helpman is a leading architect of the broader framework, including Helpman–Melitz–Yeaple on exports versus FDI. Redding's contributions are substantial and more quantitative or spatial, so I do not propose him in the core group. Bernard, Eaton and Jensen are not on this credited list, which complicates the attribution.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation and extension, with broad adoption in empirical trade and policy analysis.
uncertainties: Overlap with the trade candidates in B037 and B047, including Helpman's presence in B047.
Credit relative to empirical firm-level work by authors outside this credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki–Moore (1997) formalised how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks into credit cycles. This is a core building block of modern macro-financial models and is central to analysis of the financial crisis and its aftermath. The conceptual contribution is clear and general.
assessment.attribution: The credit-cycle mechanism is attributable to Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler and Gilchrist contributed the financial-accelerator and empirical line, with Bernanke, who is not listed here and already holds a prize for related work. Limiting the proposal to two keeps the credit sharply tied to the originating paper.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of influence, with renewed relevance after 2008. This is fully mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the 2022 prize (Bernanke–Diamond–Dybvig) as having already covered the financial-frictions field.
Whether Gertler should be included in the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The microfounded New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities underlies modern monetary-policy analysis and central-bank practice. This includes Calvo pricing, policy rules and the optimal-policy synthesis. Its policy and intellectual influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the hardest issue. Calvo supplied the pricing mechanism, Taylor the policy rule and staggered contracts, and Woodford the integrated theory of interest and prices. Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets made major contributions to estimation and the canonical model, so many deserving names are left out.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and tested over decades, including through the 2008 crisis and the 2021–23 inflation episode.
uncertainties: A three-person limit forces a contested choice among at least eight credited names.
Recent inflation and the limits of the representative-agent framework may affect the perceived robustness of the paradigm.
Overlap with the heterogeneous-agent NK candidate (B048).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the empirical evidence on trade shocks reshaped understanding of wage inequality, polarisation and the local labour-market effects of globalisation. The work has had wide influence on both academic research and public debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are central to the China-shock evidence, and Autor and Katz to the skills, technology and polarisation literature. Katz also appears in the mobility candidate and has long-standing work with Goldin, which is already honoured. The theoretical task framework has other originators outside this list, such as Acemoglu, who already holds a prize.
assessment.maturity: Core papers are 15–25 years old. The empirical findings have been debated and refined, and the central results have mostly survived.
uncertainties: Credit for the task framework is shared with laureates and non-listed authors.
Some of the China-shock magnitudes remain contested.
Overlap with prior prizes in labour economics and in technology and growth.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh–Klenow (2009) provided a tractable quantitative framework for measuring misallocation of inputs across firms and showed how much it can explain of cross-country income differences. It reorganised research in growth and development, and the approach is used in many countries.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the clear originators of the measurement framework. Restuccia and Rogerson's related macro-development work is also important, and Restuccia is credited here, so the choice to exclude him is a close call.
assessment.maturity: Roughly fifteen years of influence, with good replication across countries. The interpretation of measured wedges remains debated.
uncertainties: Measurement error and the identification of true distortions versus unobserved heterogeneity.
Whether the committee considers the field established enough relative to older candidates.
Relative standing of Restuccia.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave credible new measurements of intergenerational mobility, its geography, and the causal effects of neighbourhoods. This changed both the empirical standards and the policy discussion on opportunity. The work is closely related to long-standing theoretical interest in mobility and inequality.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear lead across the programme. Hendren is central to the neighbourhood-effects results and Friedman to the mobility and teacher-value-added studies. Katz appears in other candidates and in the Moving to Opportunity work, so credit is shared across a large team.
assessment.maturity: The core results are about a decade old. They are influential but have had less time to be tested in the long run, and Chetty's work spans many areas, including the tax candidate in B035.
uncertainties: Timing: the committee may prefer a longer record of replication and long-run follow-up.
The scope question of whether the prize would recognise a method and data advance versus a distinct discovery.
Large collaborative teams complicate attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Mian and Sufi documented the role of household leverage and credit supply in the housing boom and the depth of the Great Recession. Their work links micro data to macroeconomic outcomes and shaped post-crisis understanding of household debt.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the clear joint originators of the household-debt programme. Campbell's contributions to household finance and asset pricing are distinct and are better judged under a different heading.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen years since the key papers. The empirical findings are well replicated but some interpretation, including credit supply versus demand, is still debated.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is yet seen as a discovery of Nobel scale or an important empirical programme.
Contested identification of credit-supply effects.
Overlap with the 2022 prize and the other macro-finance candidates.
